sections.h2: Ways to sell a Dearborn Heights house
sections.html:
You can hire an agent, arrange a sale yourself with a buyer you found, or accept an as-is purchase from an investor paying cash. Whichever you pick, the Wayne County register of deeds records the deed, transfer tax is paid at recording, and the city asks sellers to complete a few steps of its own.

A well-kept house can sell through a normal listing. Deferred repairs, a deceased owner's estate or a tenant dispute often point toward a cash sale, since the buyer absorbs the condition and the closing timeline is shorter.

  • Listing: the biggest buyer pool, plus inspection and financing contingencies.
  • Direct sale: fewer fees, with more paperwork landing on you.
  • Investor purchase: as-is, a quicker close and a price that reflects repairs.

Dearborn Heights is an inner-ring suburb about 12 miles west of downtown Detroit, packed into under 12 square miles. It counted 63,292 residents in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 4.1% lower, so the city is shrinking slightly. The average household has 2.76 people, and the 2020 count showed 24,076 housing units with only 4.9% vacant. Median age was 35.7, and about a quarter of residents were under 18, which favors family buyers who care about bedrooms, yards and school zones.

Because so many residents speak another language at home, marketing in more than one language can widen your buyer pool.

The southern part of the city lies in the Ecorse Creek watershed, where the area around the creek is subject to flooding, and the north drains toward the Rouge River. The Building Department posts a flood zone map, so check your parcel before you price the house. Buyers tend to ask about three items: the flood history of the lot, how old the roof and furnace are, and the school district. Have answers ready for each.

The city is split among five public districts, which makes the exact address matter. North-end residents are usually in Crestwood School District or Dearborn Public Schools, and south-end residents in Westwood Community Schools or the Dearborn Heights School District No. 7. A small part falls within Wayne-Westland Community Schools and Taylor School District. Put the district in your listing, since buyers who search by school filter on it.

sections.h2: What the city asks sellers to do
sections.html:
If the house is your primary residence, you must rescind the Principal Residence Exemption when it sells. The title company may hand you the Request to Rescind at closing, and if not, the Assessor's Office at 313-791-3460 can give it to you. This applies even to a quit claim deed with no title company involved.

Contact the Building Department at 6045 Fenton (313-791-3470) to learn which inspections the sale requires, since the city offers a residential certificate inspection application. Call the Water Department as well for a final meter reading.

Treat the three city contacts as a package. Each one answers a different question: the Assessor's Office handles the exemption and the transfer affidavit, the Building Department handles inspections and the flood map, and the Water Department handles the meter. Making all three calls in the same sitting saves you from learning about a requirement the week before closing.

On the buyer's side, the Property Transfer Affidavit has to reach the assessor inside 45 days of the deed. A late filing can cost up to $200 on a primary residence, and as much as $4,000 on other residential property.

The county's recording fee rose on January 1, 2026, the first change since 1996. A deed now costs $26, plus the $4 state survey and remonumentation fee, for $30 on each document, however long it is.

At the counter, tax is taken the moment the deed is handed in, and the office wants cash, a check or a money order made payable to it. Tax is 55 cents per $500 for the county plus $3.75 per $500 for the state, which works out to $8.60 per $1,000 of price, and the seller pays.

A warranty deed needs the Wayne County Treasurer's certification that taxes are paid before it can be recorded. Every deed has to name the price or cite the exemption statute, and it needs original signatures and a notary acknowledgment. Calling the Register of Deeds at (313) 224-5851 before submission can prevent a rejection.

sections.h2: When an investor purchase beats a listing
sections.html:
It fits when the house has problems a retail buyer would refuse, when a deadline looms, or when you would rather skip showings. Typical cases are a house needing mechanical work, an inherited property, a landlord ready to exit, and a home with open city inspection items.

Also think about the estate case. When the owner has died, confirm who has authority to sign before anyone talks price, because a deed signed by the wrong person cannot be recorded cleanly. An investor who buys inherited houses regularly will know this process, but you should still ask for the steps in writing.

Before accepting, get the offer on paper, find out who pays recording and title costs, and make sure the buyer will cooperate with the city's rescind and inspection steps. A second quote costs little and shows whether the first is reasonable. Ask also how the buyer handles the Wayne County Treasurer's tax certification, since recording stalls without it.

1. Call the Building Department at 313-791-3470 and ask which inspections apply to your address.
  2. Check the flood zone map and gather any water-damage records.
  3. Ask the Assessor's Office at 313-791-3460 for the rescind form.
  4. Request a final meter reading from the Water Department.
  5. Confirm the treasurer's certification for a warranty deed and the deed's price or exemption language.
  6. Remind the buyer about the 45-day affidavit.

None of these steps is hard on its own, but they come from different offices, so start the calls early. A seller who has everything lined up can close quickly whether the buyer is paying cash or using a loan.

faqs.q: Is a certificate inspection required to sell in Dearborn Heights?
faqs.a: The city directs sellers to its Building Department to find out which inspections apply, and it offers a residential certificate inspection application. Call 313-791-3470 before you list so you know what is required for your address.

faqs.q: Which taxes hit the seller at Dearborn Heights closing?
faqs.a: The county's 55 cents and the state's $3.75 on each $500 of price add up to $8.60 per $1,000. The seller pays it, and it is collected as the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Who files the Property Transfer Affidavit?
faqs.a: The buyer sends it to the Assessor's Office, and it is due 45 calendar days after the deed is signed. A late filing can carry a fine, so the seller should remind the buyer at closing.

faqs.q: What if I buy my next home before this one sells?
faqs.a: Michigan allows only one principal residence exemption, so you must rescind the Dearborn Heights exemption once you move out. The new city may ask for a stamped copy of the rescind form before it grants an exemption on the new home.

faqs.q: Is a flood-prone Dearborn Heights house sellable?
faqs.a: Yes. Parts of the south end sit in the Ecorse Creek watershed where flooding occurs, so check the city's flood zone map and tell your buyer what you know about water in the basement.
